title: The number that leaked a console

blocks.heading: The number that leaked a console
text: Berlin, 29 December 2010. Three researchers put Sony's PlayStation 3 code-signing key on a slide.
They did not break ECDSA. They used it correctly, twice.

blocks.heading: The rule attached to $k$
text: Caleb's wallet drew a fresh secret $k$ to sign the 0.05 BTC payment. The signing equation carries one condition that is easy to miss:

blocks.caption: $k$ must be unpredictable **and never repeated**. The second half is the part that gets skipped.

blocks.heading: What Sony shipped
text: The function that was supposed to produce a fresh $k$ for each signature produced the same value every time.

blocks.label: the shape of the bug
blocks.code:
def get_nonce():
    return 0xdeadbeef      # placeholder that shipped

blocks.heading: The tell is public
text: $r$ comes only from $k$. Same $k$, same $r$ - visible in any two signatures.

blocks.alt: Two signature rows; the r column is highlighted and identical in both, while the s values differ
blocks.caption: Nothing here is secret. Both signatures were published in the ordinary way.

blocks.heading: Subtract them
text: Both signatures contain the term $rd$, and it is _the same term_. Subtracting one equation from the other deletes the private key:

blocks.heading: Then put it back
text: With $k$ known, the original equation has exactly one unknown left.

blocks.caption: Two modular inversions. On a laptop, this is instant.

blocks.question: $r$ is published in every signature ever made and gives nothing away. Why is seeing the same one twice fatal?
answer: One signature is one equation with two unknowns, $k$ and $d$. Unsolvable, and that is the security.
A repeated $r$ announces that the same $k$ was used, which turns two signatures into two equations in the _same_ two unknowns. Solvable systems have solutions.

blocks.heading: Run on a real key
text: Signing two messages with one reused nonce, then recovering the key from the signatures alone:

blocks.label: tools/visuals/nonce-reuse.py
blocks.code:
signature 1   r d7be8435...641e   s 5c5f4ed1...68bf
signature 2   r d7be8435...641e   s 716f5b16...057f
recovered d   5f3a9c11...b8f1   match: True

blocks.heading: What it cost
text: The recovered key was the one the console trusted. Anything signed with it - any program at all - the PS3 accepted as Sony's own.
A firmware update can change a key. It cannot un-publish one.

blocks.heading: The same bug, on a chain
text: Bitcoin.org issued an advisory: Android's `SecureRandom` could initialise badly, and wallets on affected phones signed with repeating nonces.
Duplicate $r$ values appeared on the public chain. The coins behind them were taken.

blocks.title: A chain makes this worse, structurally
text: Sony's signatures had to be collected. Bitcoin's are broadcast to everyone and stored forever.
Scanning the entire history for two signatures that share an $r$ is cheap, needs no access to anything, and works retroactively on a mistake made years ago.

blocks.heading: The fix removes the requirement
text: RFC 6979, published the same month as the advisory, derives $k$ from the private key and the message hash with HMAC.
The signer needs no randomness at signing time at all. There is no entropy source left to fail.

blocks.question: Deterministic nonces mean signing the same message twice gives byte-identical signatures. Is that not itself a leak?
answer: No. $k$ is derived from the message _and_ the private key, so nobody without $d$ can recompute it. The output is predictable only to the signer.
It also makes signing reproducible, which means a test suite can catch a broken implementation. BIP-340 uses the same approach for Schnorr signatures.

blocks.heading: The quiet version of this failure
text: Full reuse is loud. Bias is not.

If $k$ is merely _slightly_ non-uniform - a few predictable top bits - lattice reduction recovers $d$ from a large collection of ordinary signatures. No repeat is needed. Published attacks have worked with under one bit of leakage per signature.

blocks.heading: One sentence worth keeping
text: The mathematics was never the weak point; the number nobody thinks about was.
Caleb's wallet uses RFC 6979, so this does not happen to him. Next: turning Nora's public key into something she can paste into an email without losing €4,150 to a typo.
